summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: SRS (now DCF) owed the reporting children an actionable duty of care because 33 V.S.A. § 4915 imposes mandatory investigative acts for the protection of a particular class, and sovereign immunity did not bar the negligence suit.
key_cases.relevance: Section 4915's mandatory language - investigation 'shall' commence, 'shall' include a home visit and child interview - is the standard Sabia enforces at the accept-for-investigation decision.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that SRS had a duty to protect plaintiffs under the circumstances of this case.

key_cases.case_name: Willis S. Sheldon, Individually and as Administrator of the Estate of Dezirae Sheldon v. Nicholas Ruggiero
key_cases.holding: Summary judgment for a DCF administrative reviewer was affirmed because the mandated-reporter duty under 33 V.S.A. § 4913(a) is triggered only by reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused, and a repetitious allegation adding nothing new did not supply it.
key_cases.relevance: The Court emphasizes DCF's separate statutory obligation under §§ 4915 and 4915b to investigate all potential sources of a child's injuries.
key_cases.quote: In this context, as a matter of law, defendant did not have reasonable cause to make a report.

key_cases.case_name: Tina Stocker v. State of Vermont
key_cases.holding: Judgment as a matter of law for the State was affirmed: the only non-discretionary DCF duty supporting a damages action is the 33 V.S.A. § 4915 duty to record a report and make an initial determination whether it is valid, assessment and investigation under §§ 4915a and 4915b are discretionary and within sovereign immunity, and plaintiffs could not show the recording failures proximately caused the children's continued abuse.
key_cases.relevance: It separates the mandatory acceptance decision from the discretionary conduct of the assessment or investigation under §§ 4915a and 4915b, and holds the Legislature foreclosed any private right of action as to the latter.
key_cases.quote: any implied right of action against DCF based in this statutory scheme is limited to violations of mandatory duties pursuant to § 4915

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to document the safety determination and safety plan on the SDM Safety Assessment
timeline_requirements.starts_from: First in-person interview with the family
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days to conclude an investigation; 45 days to complete an assessment, or 60 days with written justification and supervisor approval
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Opening of the child safety intervention (the investigation or assessment track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024); the policy allows an investigation to stay open past 60 days while a law enforcement or criminal case is unresolved, and an assessment extension may not exceed 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)). Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track by statute (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
